title: {{NAME}} and the Royal Fairy Council
moral: Great leaders listen to voices much smaller than their own.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} was sent to the Greenwood Court as the princess's page, which mostly involved carrying things and standing near doors.

He was very good at both. He was also very good at noticing things.

What he noticed in the first week: tiny golden lights in the throne room rafters that weren't candles. Doors swinging open with no breeze. The princess always pausing before major decisions, tilting her head slightly, as if listening to something nobody else could hear.

pages.content:
He found out the truth on a Thursday, when he was late delivering a message and cut through the garden maze.

At the maze's centre: a circle of fairies, no bigger than his hand, seated around a tiny round table. Across from them, sitting cross-legged on the grass in her best gown, was Princess Seraphine.

The fairies were all talking at once. The princess was taking notes.

{{NAME}} stopped breathing.

One fairy looked directly at him. "You," she said. "Sit down. We need a second opinion."

pages.content:
The issue, it turned out, was a new law the princess was considering: a tax on riverside trade that seemed logical in the palace but would devastate the fairy settlements in the reed beds.

{{NAME}} knew the reed beds. His grandmother had lived near them.

"The reeds flood in spring," he said carefully. "The fairy settlements move up the bank. If the tax forces the traders to use the northern road, the reed bed communities lose half their food supply for three months."

The princess stopped writing. The fairies looked at him.

"How does he know that?" one asked.

"He notices things," said the princess.

pages.content:
The council ran for two hours.

{{NAME}} did not contribute often, but when he did, it was useful. He knew which roads flooded, which markets ran on what schedule, which human communities lived nearest to the fairy settlements.

At the end, the princess rewrote the law to exempt riverside traders for six months of each year.

The head fairy, whose name was something like the sound bells make in fog, reached up and put a single tiny hand on {{NAME}}'s finger.

"You may return next council," she said, which he understood was a high honour.

pages.content:
Walking home from the palace that evening, {{NAME}} felt the weight of the day settling in his bones: the good kind of tired.

He had carried messages all morning and changed a law all afternoon.

In his small room above the stables, he sat on his bed and looked at his finger where the fairy had touched it. A tiny golden ring, no bigger than a thread, was just visible in the lamplight.

He lay down and closed his eyes.

Somewhere in the reed beds, he thought he could hear tiny voices: talking, planning, safe.
